To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the structure of cation salmon trypsin, a non-psychophilic enzyme, has been solved and that the structure is similar to that of the psychrophillic anionic salmon trypein.
the cationic salmon enzyme has an enhanced surface hydrophilic character, a high content of surface exposed methionine residues, and a low overall hydrophobic character.

(1) CST is structurally very similar to AST and BT, with the largest r.m.s. difference in main-chain atoms of 0.7 A; (2) the two salmon trypsin enzymes have a similar surface structure, which differs significantly from that of BT; (3) CST and AST are more similar to each other than either is to BT
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural basis for the observed differences between CST, AST and BT, with a particular emphasis on the structural determinants for the observed differences in thermostability.
the structural basis of cold-adaptation and the role of the autolysis loop in the thermostability of the trypsins.
the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms of cold-adaptation in enzymes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cold-adapted salmon trypsin has evolved to be more hydrophilic than the non-psychrophiic salmon trypin, while the latter has evolved to be even more hydrophilic compared with bovine trypin.
the structural differences between the two salmon trypsins are not sufficient to account for the observed differences in thermostability.
the psychrophilicity of a trypsin cannot be explained by its overall hydrophobic content, nor by the presence or absence of a calcium-binding loop.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CST and AST have a higher content of charged surface residues, and that the autolysis loop is more exposed to solvent in CST than in BT.
the observed structural differences between the two salmon trypsins are too minor to explain their difference in catalytic efficiency.
the cold-adapted enzymes have a more open surface, a lower hydrophobicity, and a higher methionine content.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the structural features associated with psychrophilic adaptation in salmon trypsin are not confined to the active-site region, but rather are spread throughout the entire protein.
the observed differences in thermostability of the two salmon enzymes are not related to the observed differences in surface hydrophobicity, but rather to the presence of a calcium-binding loop.
the differences in the surface properties of the three trypsins are not sufficient to explain the differences in thermostability.
